title: Wafer & yield
summary: Why defects make big dies expensive, and why chiplets help.

links.then: fewer work, so big designs split into chiplets in one package

links.why: only dies that pass test get packaged
yield sets the cost per chip

ideas.how: small dies dodge defects, so splitting a big design into chiplets wastes less

then: The biggest die so far holds {biggestTr} transistors ({biggest}). Bigger dies catch more defects.

learn.plain: Picture raindrops falling on a tiled floor: any tile hit by a drop is ruined. Big tiles get hit more often, so cutting a design into smaller tiles (chiplets) wastes less.
learn.engineer: Common yield models are Poisson e^(−AD₀), Murphy ((1 − e^(−AD₀)) ÷ AD₀)² and negative binomial (1 + AD₀/α)^(−α), where α captures how defects cluster. Defect density falls along a learning curve as a node ramps. Redundancy (spare memory rows, fused-off cores) and binning recover partly defective dies, which is why many products ship with some units disabled.

quiz.q: What happens to yield as die area grows, at the same defect density?
options: It does not depend on area
quiz.why: Poisson yield is e^(−A·D₀): a bigger area catches more defects.

quiz.q: Why can chiplets lower the cost of a working chip?
options: Smaller dies yield better, and only known-good dies are combined
quiz.why: The trade-off is extra area and cost for die-to-die links and advanced packaging.
